findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and can be reused
findings.body: When recovery codes are stored in local (Keycloak DB) storage, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid() removes the used code so each code is single-use. With this change, when the credential lives in a federated user storage, validation goes through user.credentialManager().isValid(), which only delegates to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid() — a read-only check that cannot mutate or remove the used code. There is no subsequent updateCredential call to persist the consumption either. As a result, a recovery code backed by user storage remains valid forever and can be replayed indefinitely, defeating the one-time-use security property of recovery codes.

findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById does not remove a federated recovery-codes credential when all codes are used
findings.body: After the change, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential() can return a credential coming from federated user storage. When allCodesUsed() is true, the code calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(...), which only removes credentials from Keycloak's local storage; for a federated credential this is a no-op (the id is not a locally stored credential). The exhausted credential therefore remains in the user storage and will keep being returned by getFederatedCredentialsStream(). To remove it from user storage the code would need disableCredentialType / a provider-side removal path.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are handed to user storage, unlike local storage which stores hashes
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) into a UserCredentialModel and passes it to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). When the credential ends up in local storage, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel stores each code hashed (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode). When it ends up in user storage, the external provider receives and — as the updated BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage demonstrates — persists the plaintext codes, and validates them with plain string equality. Any user storage following this contract will hold recovery codes in cleartext, so a compromise of the external store exposes all valid recovery codes, a weaker security posture than the local-storage path with no documentation warning about it.

findings.title: Optional.get() on credential lookup throws NoSuchElementException instead of a handled error when credential is absent
findings.body: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) may return Optional.empty() (e.g., the credential was removed between configuredFor() and form rendering, or a federated provider's getCredentials() failed to deserialize and silently dropped the entry, as BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does on IOException). Calling credentialModelOpt.get() then throws NoSuchElementException, producing an unhandled 500 error on the login page instead of a graceful authentication error. The code should handle the empty case explicitly.
